title: Report
description: User-initiated, and filed after the attempt so it can carry whether the fix worked. Deliberately carries no timestamp and no incident id: a report must not be linkable back to the run that produced it. `dropped` names what was withheld, so the omission is visible rather than silent, and `observed` and `stated` are separate so a measurement and a claim can never wear the same name. Free text travels only in `description`, only when the user has seen it and agreed, and only with a destination named.

resolved_by.description: A measurement, not metadata. A small local model solving something from public knowledge means the information was available and the product surface failed to convey it — a UX defect rather than a knowledge gap.

observed.description: Readings, already coarsened by the generalisation policy. **Measurements only.** A value a person supplied is never here, so a recipient that ignores `stated` sees fewer facts rather than a claim it mistakes for a measurement.

stated.description: What a person supplied — typed, chosen, or answering a probe the skill declared `human` — coarsened by the same policy. Kept apart from `observed` rather than flagged inside it, because the failure to design against is a consumer that does not look: ignoring a flag turns a claim into a measurement, whereas ignoring this map only loses facts. A publisher needs the difference — a solution that matched on a measurement and failed is a defect in their rule; one that matched on a typed value and failed may be nothing of the sort. A null value means supplied but withheld: free text a person typed never travels, but that somebody supplied it is a property of the report rather than anything about them, and it is what decides whether an outcome says anything about a published rule.

decided_on.description: The facts the answer actually turned on — the switches taken, not every fact that was present. Empty where the producer did not say. Combined with `stated` it is what lets a publisher tell an outcome that tests their rule from one that tests whether somebody answered a question correctly, and only the first is evidence about them.

description.description: Free-text answers the user chose to send, each labelled with the probe that asked for it. A publisher may ask a free-text question — an error message is the single most useful thing they can receive and the one thing no machine can generalise — and the answer is withheld by default, shown to the user verbatim and editable, and travels only if they agree. `stated` still names the probe with a null value, so a recipient can always tell a question was asked even when the answer did not travel.

description_consent.description: Its own consent, naming who receives it. `granted` must be true, `destination` names the recipient, and `granted_at` is a year-month — the same granularity as the pseudonym, because a precise time would relink a report to the run that produced it, which is the one thing the report format refuses. Enforced by a database CHECK on the receiving side, not by a handler.

pseudonym.description: Per vendor and per epoch, so a recipient can count, rate-limit and block without linking this client across vendors or across months. A recipient counting distinct reporters must count distinct pseudonyms; counting submissions cannot tell five people from one person reporting five times.
